relevant_contributions.explanation: This theorem is the central result of the LATE framework. It shows that when treatment effects are heterogeneous and compliance is incomplete, the IV estimand—the ratio of the reduced-form effect to the first-stage effect—identifies the average causal effect for compliers, i.e., those who change treatment status in response to the instrument. The assumptions are: (1) the instrument is as good as randomly assigned, (2) the instrument has a nonzero effect on treatment (relevance), (3) the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment (exclusion restriction), and (4) monotonicity, meaning no one is a defier (who would take treatment when assigned control but not when assigned treatment). This result clarifies what can be learned from IV designs and provides a transparent interpretation of the estimand.

The source states that under the exclusion restriction, ITT is a diluted treatment effect, and cites Hernán and Hernandez-Diaz (2012) for the discussion that this can make unsafe treatments appear safe (p128).

Cross-fitting is defined in Section 3 (p24) as K-fold sample splitting with averaging, and the paper explains it removes overfitting bias while retaining efficiency (p6). The term 'cross-fitting' is coined by the authors, building on earlier sample-splitting ideas (p10).
The paper applies DML to estimate the effect of 401(k) eligibility, showing flexible confounding control, illustrating practical use (p42-43).
Section 6.1 (p40-41) reports DML estimates of the cash bonus effect on unemployment duration as negative and significant across methods, consistent with prior studies.
The source uses the dilution argument to motivate LATE as a more informative estimand (p128).
The paper applies DML to the Pennsylvania experiment, producing sensible estimates, illustrating practical use (p40-41).
Remark 4.3 (p33) and Remark 5.2 (p37) explicitly state that cross-fitting relaxes sparsity conditions from (s_g)^2 + (s_m)^2 << N to s_g * s_m << N for lasso-based nuisance estimation.

Section 6.3 (p45) describes applying DML to estimate the effect of institutions on GDP using settler mortality as an instrument, following Acemoglu et al. (2001). The paper does not report detailed results but highlights applicability.
The paper shows the conditional moment framework with a specific weighting matrix yields the same orthogonal score for the partially linear model (p21, p32).

Remark 4.2 (p33) states under homoscedasticity the asymptotic variance reduces to the semiparametric efficiency bound for the partially linear model. Theorem 5.1 (p37) states ATE and ATTE estimators are efficient reaching Hahn (1998) bound.
Corollary 3.1 (p28) states confidence intervals based on DML estimators have asymptotic coverage uniformly over a class of probability measures, following from uniform asymptotic normality.
The paper shows cross-fitting weakens sparsity requirements, making DML applicable in broader settings, supporting the general theory (p33, p37).
The paper shows DML achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound in specific cases, indicating optimality (p33, p37).
The paper applies the general DML theory to LATE estimation using an orthogonal score, proving root-N consistency and normality (p38-39).

Definition 3.3 (p31) proposes median-based aggregation over multiple splits, and Corollary 3.3 states it is first-order equivalent to the single-split estimator. The paper recommends medians for robustness.

Section 2.2.4 (p20-21) presents the conditional moment restrictions framework with orthogonal scores constructed via weighting and moment selection functions, achieving semiparametric efficiency with appropriate choices (Chamberlain 1992).
The paper states sample splitting plays a key role in guaranteeing remainder terms vanish, essential for asymptotic normality (p5, p28).
The source discusses LATE as a complement to ITT in medical trials (p128, p130).

Theorem 5.1 (p37) states DML estimators for ATE and ATTE are root-N consistent, asymptotically normal, and efficient, reaching the Hahn (1998) bound. The orthogonal scores are provided in Section 5.1 (p36).
The paper applies DML to estimate the effect of institutions on GDP, showing applicability in structural IV models (p45).

Section 2.2.3 (p19) describes the concentrating-out approach: maximize expected criterion over nuisance, then differentiate with respect to target, yielding an orthogonal score. The paper shows it works for infinite-dimensional nuisance parameters.
The paper argues Donsker conditions are inappropriate for high-dimensional ML, and cross-fitting avoids these conditions (p7, p10).
Theorem 5.2 (p39) states DML estimators for LATE are root-N consistent and asymptotically normal under conditions on nuisance estimation rates. The orthogonal score is provided in Section 5.2 (p38).
The paper proves asymptotic normality holds uniformly, allowing uniformly valid confidence intervals, a stronger result than pointwise normality (p28).
The source argues that LATE is a more informative estimand than ITT in medical trials with incomplete adherence, citing authors like McNamee (2009) and Shrier et al. (2014) (p128, p130).
The paper shows adding the influence function adjustment to the naive score produces the orthogonal score for the partially linear model (p23, p32).

Section 6.2 (p42-43) reports DML estimates of 401(k) eligibility effect on net financial assets around $7,000-$9,000, substantially attenuated from the uncontrolled estimate of $19,559, indicating confounding control matters.

The paper argues Donsker conditions are unsuitable for high-dimensional ML because entropy grows with dimension (p7, p10). It provides an example of a linear model with Euclidean ball parameter space where entropy grows with p_N.
The paper applies the general DML theory to the partially linear model using the orthogonal score, proving root-N consistency and normality (p32-33).
The paper demonstrates regularization bias in naive ML plug-in estimators with a decomposition and simulation (p3, p4). The claim that the bias term diverges is supported by the text.
The paper proves both DML1 and DML2 estimators satisfy the same asymptotic properties, with DML2 recommended for small samples (p25, p28).
The paper shows the median estimator is first-order equivalent to the single-split estimator, supporting practical use of DML (p31).
The paper shows the concentrating-out method applied to the partially linear model produces the score (D - m(X))(Y - Dθ - g(X)), same as in (1.5) (p19, p32).

The score (Y - Dθ - g(X))(D - m(X)) is presented as Neyman orthogonal for the partially linear model in Section 4.1 (p32) and derived in the introduction (p4). The paper shows it removes regularization bias.
Definition 3.2 (p25) defines DML2 as solving a pooled equation across folds, and Remark 3.1 recommends DML2 over DML1 for better small-sample behavior due to more stable pooled Jacobian.
The paper shows overfitting bias persists even with orthogonal scores, motivating sample splitting (p6, p8).
The paper applies the general DML theory to ATE estimation using orthogonal scores, proving root-N consistency and efficiency (p36-37).

Section 2.2.5 (p22-23) describes constructing orthogonal scores by adding influence function adjustments to the original score, building on Newey (1994). The paper illustrates this with the partially linear model.

Theorem 3.1 (p28) states DML estimators concentrate in 1/sqrt(N) neighborhood and are approximately linear and Gaussian uniformly over P in P_N. The proof relies on Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting as described in the paper.
